_comment: Guided tour for the flow-map tool. Steps point at real controls and wait for the user to press them -- there is deliberately no 'do it for me' button, because someone who watched a button being pressed has not learned where it is. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: What this tool measures
steps.text:
A flow map is one velocity vector per place in the image — where the sample is moving, and how fast. Nothing here is fitted: the velocity is read off where a correlation peak is, not off a parameter released in a transport model.

Nine steps, about a minute. You press the buttons; the tour only points at them.

steps.title: Start with data you can check
steps.text:
The hard part of a flow map is knowing whether to believe it: arrows appear over a picture and there is nothing to compare them with.

So start with a simulated scan whose flow is known — laminar flow through a channel, fastest in the middle and zero at the walls. It is a real photon stream, written as an ordinary PTU.

await.hint: Press 🧪 Load demo. The first time it simulates the scan, which takes about half a minute; the status bar counts the frames.

steps.title: The file is now selected
steps.text: The demo has been written and loaded, and its scanner settings came with it. Any TIFF stack or photon stream can go here instead — it just needs at least three frames, since a flow map measures what moved between them.

steps.title: The scanner clock is the measurement
steps.text:
A velocity is a distance over a time, and both come from here — not from the image. The frame time is the clock a STICS velocity is measured against, and the pixel size converts pixels into µm. An error in either scales every arrow by the same factor with nothing looking wrong.

The demo filled these in. For a real file, take them from the acquisition software.

steps.title: Tile size: the resolution of the map
steps.text:
Each arrow is computed from one square sub-region. A small tile localizes the flow but holds few molecules and leaves the peak little room to travel; a large tile averages distinct flows into a single arrow.

Several focus waists across is the usual compromise — 24 pixels here, about 2.4 µm.

steps.title: Lags: the trap worth knowing
steps.text:
The peak travels further the more frames you look ahead — and it must stay inside its tile. A correlation map is periodic, so a peak driven past the edge does not disappear: it wraps round to the other side, where a straight line fits a confident velocity pointing the wrong way.

Tiles where that happened are refused and counted rather than reported. If the summary says tiles were refused, use fewer lags or a bigger tile.

steps.title: Now measure
steps.text: Every tile gets its own correlation carpet, its peak is tracked across the lag range, and a straight line through those peaks is the velocity.

steps.title: Read the arrows
steps.text:
Direction first — that is the part a correlation measurement gets right even where the magnitude is conservative. The demo flows along +x, fastest in the middle of the frame.

Colour runs from cool for the slowest tile to warm for the fastest, and the caption underneath says how many arrows survived the quality threshold.

steps.title: Check it against the truth
steps.text:
The profile collapses the field to one curve across the frame, with the simulated truth drawn beside it in green.

The shape should match — parabolic, peaking in the middle. The recovered magnitude reads about 20 % low, and that is a real property of the method, not a bug: where the flow shears inside a tile the correlation peak is smeared as well as displaced, and a smaller tile does not fix it. A flow map is a reliable picture of where and a conservative estimate of how fast.

steps.title: Before you believe a real map
steps.text:
Four checks, in the order that catches most:

1. Did any tile escape? The summary says so. Shorten the lag range.
2. Does a static region go blank as you raise this threshold? Peak jitter fitted to a line is always some velocity.
3. Does the other estimator agree? Pair correlation shares no kernel with STICS.
4. Does reversing the flow reverse the arrows? Nothing else catches a mirrored axis.

The ? button beside the guide has the long version.
